original_description: Mistake-proofing for software — Shigeo Shingo's poka-yoke (poke yoke, mistake-proofing, error-proofing) method applied to code, process, and AI agents. Use this skill whenever someone wants to make a mistake impossible rather than merely caught: designing an API or schema so it cannot be misused, auditing code for footguns and easy-to-misuse signatures, making invalid states unrepresentable, installing pre-commit/CI/lint/database guardrails, hardening a repo against agent-written mistakes, or turning a bug, outage, or postmortem into a device that prevents that whole class of error from recurring. Trigger it on phrases like "poka-yoke", "poke yoke", "mistake-proof", "error-proof", "foolproof this", "make it impossible to", "footgun", "easy to misuse", "make invalid states unrepresentable", "guardrails", "prevent this from happening again", "how do we stop someone doing X by accident", and on incident retros or hardening work even when none of those words appear.

final_description: Use when documentation, instructions, or agreements aren't being followed and the user wants mechanical enforcement instead. Key patterns: "CLAUDE.md says X but it still does Y", "we agreed to X but people don't", "had another incident where someone did X", "designing this so you can't accidentally X", "paranoid we've missed a filter somewhere". Applies to: API/SDK signatures that prevent caller mistakes, state machines where invalid transitions are unrepresentable, pre-commit/CI hooks that block bad commits, agent guardrails via hooks, multi-tenant query scoping, prod-vs-staging protection. The core signal is wanting a structural fix rather than more documentation — making the wrong thing impossible, not just discouraged. Also triggers on: poka-yoke, mistake-proof, error-proof, footgun, guardrails, "make invalid states unrepresentable".

history.description: Use this skill when someone wants to make a mistake impossible through design, not documentation. Trigger on: API/schema design questions asking how to prevent misuse ("so people can't screw it up", "so you can't accidentally X"); state machines or type design where invalid states should be unrepresentable; process compliance failures where instructions, agreements, or docs aren't being followed ("we said X but people still do Y", "CLAUDE.md says X but it keeps doing Y"); repeated incidents or near-misses asking how to prevent recurrence structurally; multi-tenant/authz concerns about missing filters; wanting mechanical enforcement over human memory. Core signal: frustration that telling people (or agents) not to do something isn't working, and desire for a structural fix. Also trigger on explicit terms: poka-yoke, mistake-proof, error-proof, footgun, guardrails.
